messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kai Jensen's eyes would glaze over when he tried to recount the night he was mugged on his way home from a late shift at the Coast Guard station. "It's like trying to describe a dream," he'd say, frustration etched on his face. His girlfriend, Rachel, had grown accustomed to seeing him struggle to put words to the memories that haunted him. She'd encourage him to keep talking, hoping something would click into place, but it rarely did. Sometimes, fragments of that night would surface in vivid detail – the sound of footsteps behind him, the feeling of hands grabbing his shoulders, the crunch of gravel beneath his palms as he fell. But these moments were disjointed, unmoored from any coherent narrative. Other times, Kai could recall entire stretches of the evening with eerie precision: walking home, lost in thought; noticing a group of teenagers lingering by the alleyway; quickening his pace. Yet even these memories felt strangely detached, as if they belonged to someone else entirely. Kai's inability to piece together that night's events had become a constant source of unease. He'd find himself ruminating on what might have happened during those lost moments – the worst-case scenarios playing out like gruesome tableaux in his mind. These speculations often left him feeling numb, disconnected from his own emotions and experiences. As the months went by, Kai began to notice changes in his daily routine. He started taking longer routes home from work, avoiding alleys and dimly lit side streets. His patrol shifts became more grueling; every snap of a twig or shout from a bystander made him jump. Rachel noticed that he was pulling away, cancelling plans at the last minute or opting for solitary activities instead of spending time with her. The Coast Guard's latest training exercises had also become increasingly challenging. Kai struggled to focus during drills, his mind wandering back to those disjointed memories and the fears they fueled. His commanding officer called him in for a chat, expressing concern about Kai's performance – and that's when it hit him: he couldn't keep going on like this. With Rachel's encouragement, Kai finally made an appointment with a therapist, hoping someone could help him untangle the knotted memories that had taken over his life. As he sat in the waiting room, filling out forms and fidgeting with his cap, he couldn't shake the feeling of being trapped – stuck in this endless loop of fragmented recollections and numbing fear.
